claim: By default, the log files and digest files CloudTrail delivers to your bucket are encrypted with server-side encryption with a KMS key (SSE-KMS); if you do not enable SSE-KMS encryption, they are encrypted with SSE-S3.
q: How does CloudTrail encrypt log files in S3 by default?
v: server-side encryption with a KMS key (SSE-KMS)
n: Conflict with the CloudTrail FAQ, which says log files are encrypted with S3 server-side encryption (SSE) by default. The user guide and the how-it-works page say the console default is SSE-KMS with SSE-S3 as the fallback.
ev: By default, the log files and digest files delivered by CloudTrail to your bucket are encrypted by using [server-side encryption with a KMS key (SSE-KMS)](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/UsingKMSEncryption.html). If you don't enable SSE-KMS encryption, your log files and digest files are encrypted using [SSE-S3 encryption](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/UsingServerSideEncryption.html).

claim: When you create a trail in the CloudTrail console, event log files and digest files are encrypted with a KMS key by default; if you choose not to enable SSE-KMS encryption, they are encrypted using Amazon S3 server-side encryption (SSE).
q: What encryption does a trail created in the console use by default?
sc: per trail created in the console
ev: By default, when you create a trail in the CloudTrail console, your event log files and digest files are encrypted with a KMS key. If you choose not to enable ** SSE-KMS encryption**, your event log files and digest files are encrypted using Amazon S3 server-side encryption (SSE).

claim: The KMS key you choose to encrypt CloudTrail log files and digest files must be created in the same AWS Region as the Amazon S3 bucket that receives them.
q: In which Region must the KMS key for CloudTrail log encryption be?
v: same AWS Region as the Amazon S3 bucket
The KMS key that you choose
ev: The KMS key that you choose must be created in the same AWS Region as the Amazon S3 bucket that receives your log files and digest files.

claim: With SSE-KMS, a user needs S3 read permissions for the bucket and also a policy or role that allows decrypt permissions by the KMS key policy to read CloudTrail log files or digest files.
q: What permissions does a user need to read SSE-KMS encrypted CloudTrail logs?
v: S3 read permissions for the bucket
allows decrypt permissions by the KMS key policy
ev: A user must have S3 read permissions for the bucket that contains the log files and digest files.
A user must also have a policy or role applied that allows decrypt permissions by the KMS key policy.

claim: You can use a single KMS key to encrypt and decrypt CloudTrail log files and digest files for multiple accounts across all Regions.
q: Can one KMS key encrypt CloudTrail logs of several accounts and Regions?
ev: You can use a single KMS key to encrypt and decrypt log files and digest files for multiple accounts across all Regions.

claim: CloudTrail log file integrity validation lets you determine whether a log file was modified, deleted or unchanged after CloudTrail delivered it, using SHA-256 for hashing and SHA-256 with RSA for digital signing.
q: How can you prove that a CloudTrail log file was not changed or deleted?
v: modified, deleted, or unchanged after CloudTrail delivered it
SHA-256 for hashing and SHA-256 with RSA for digital signing
ev: To determine whether a log file was modified, deleted, or unchanged after CloudTrail delivered it, you can use CloudTrail log file integrity validation. This feature is built using industry standard algorithms: SHA-256 for hashing and SHA-256 with RSA for digital signing.

claim: When log file integrity validation is enabled, CloudTrail creates a hash for every log file it delivers and, every hour, creates and delivers a digest file that references the log files of the last hour and contains a hash of each.
q: What is a CloudTrail digest file?
v: creates a hash for every log file
This file is called a digest file
ev: When you enable log file integrity validation, CloudTrail creates a hash for every log file that it delivers. Every hour, CloudTrail also creates and delivers a file that references the log files for the last hour and contains a hash of each. This file is called a digest file.

claim: Digest files are delivered to the same Amazon S3 bucket as your log files, in a folder separate from the log files, which lets you enforce granular security policies.
q: Where does CloudTrail store digest files?
v: same Amazon S3 bucket associated with your trail
a folder separate from the log files
ev: The digest files are delivered to the same Amazon S3 bucket associated with your trail as your CloudTrail log files.
The digest files are put into a folder separate from the log files.

claim: Enabling log file integrity validation lets CloudTrail deliver digest files to your S3 bucket but does not itself validate the integrity of the files; you validate them afterwards, for example with the AWS CLI.
q: Does turning on log file validation check the files automatically?
v: does not validate the integrity of the files
ev: Enabling log file integrity validation allows CloudTrail to deliver digest log files to your Amazon S3 bucket, but does not validate the integrity of the files.
You can use the AWS CLI to validate the files in the location where CloudTrail delivered them.

claim: You can store CloudTrail log files and digest files in Amazon S3 or Amazon Glacier for an indefinite period of time, and you can use Amazon S3 MFA Delete to enhance the security of the stored digest files.
q: How long can you keep CloudTrail log files and how can you protect digest files?
v: for an indefinite period of time
ev: You can store the CloudTrail log files and digest files in Amazon S3 or Amazon Glacier securely, durably and inexpensively for an indefinite period of time. To enhance the security of the digest files stored in Amazon S3, you can use [Amazon S3 MFA Delete](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/UsingMFADelete.html).

claim: You can store CloudTrail log files in your bucket for as long as you want, and you can define Amazon S3 lifecycle rules to archive or delete log files automatically.
q: How long can trail log files stay in S3 and how do you expire them?
v: for as long as you want
ev: You can store your log files in your bucket for as long as you want. You can also define Amazon S3 lifecycle rules to archive or delete log files automatically.

claim: The CloudTrail trail default is to store log files indefinitely in the Amazon S3 bucket configured for the trail; you can use S3 object lifecycle management rules to define your own retention policy.
q: What is the default retention of CloudTrail log files in the bucket?
ev: The CloudTrail trail default is to store log files indefinitely in the Amazon S3 bucket configured for the trail. You can use the [Amazon S3 object lifecycle management rules](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/object-lifecycle-mgmt.html) to define your own retention policy to better meet your business and auditing needs.

claim: You cannot use MFA delete on the S3 bucket together with lifecycle configurations.
q: Can you combine S3 MFA delete with lifecycle rules on the CloudTrail log bucket?
v: cannot use MFA delete with lifecycle configurations
ev: You cannot use MFA delete with lifecycle configurations.

claim: You can configure CloudTrail to send update information to an Amazon SNS topic whenever a new log file has been sent to your S3 bucket; notifications are optional, and subscribers can include an Amazon SQS queue.
q: How can you be notified when CloudTrail delivers a new log file?
v: send update information to an Amazon SNS topic
ev: Notifications are optional. If you want notifications, you configure CloudTrail to send update information to an Amazon SNS topic whenever a new log file has been sent.

claim: When a trail sends events to CloudWatch Logs, CloudTrail sends only the events that match the trail settings, and it supports sending data, Insights and management events.
q: Which events does a trail send to CloudWatch Logs?
v: only the events that match your trail settings
ev: When you configure your trail to send events to CloudWatch Logs, CloudTrail sends only the events that match your trail settings. For example, if you configure your trail to log data events only, your trail sends data events only to your CloudWatch Logs log group. CloudTrail supports sending data, Insights, and management events to CloudWatch Logs.

claim: If you configure a multi-Region trail to send events to a CloudWatch Logs log group, CloudTrail sends events from all Regions to a single log group.
q: How many log groups does a multi-Region trail use in CloudWatch Logs?
v: from all Regions to a single log group
ev: | [Monitor events with CloudWatch Logs](monitor-cloudtrail-log-files-with-cloudwatch-logs.md) | You can configure your trail to send events to CloudWatch Logs. You can then use CloudWatch Logs to monitor your account for specific API calls and events. If you configure a multi-Region trail to send events to a CloudWatch Logs log group, CloudTrail sends events from all Regions to a single log group.  |

claim: To be notified of specific activity, configure your trail to send log events to CloudWatch Logs and then define CloudWatch Logs metric filters that evaluate log events for matches in terms, phrases or values, such as ConsoleLogin events.
q: How do you alarm on a specific CloudTrail event such as a console login?
ev: Configure your trail to send log events to CloudWatch Logs.
Define CloudWatch Logs metric filters to evaluate log events for matches in terms, phrases, or values. For example, you can monitor for `ConsoleLogin` events.

claim: Only the management account can configure a CloudWatch Logs log group for an organization trail using the console; the delegated administrator can do it using the AWS CLI or the CreateTrail or UpdateTrail API operations.
q: Who can configure CloudWatch Logs for an organization trail in the console?
v: Only the management account can configure
ev: Only the management account can configure a CloudWatch Logs log group for an organization trail using the console. The delegated administrator can configure a CloudWatch Logs log group using the AWS CLI or CloudTrail `CreateTrail` or `UpdateTrail` API operations.

claim: CloudTrail captures actions made directly by the user or on behalf of the user by an AWS service, so one CloudFormation CreateStack call can result in additional API calls to other services; the invokedby field shows whether an AWS service took the action.
q: Does CloudTrail also record API calls that an AWS service makes for you?
ev: CloudTrail captures actions made directly by the user or on behalf of the user by an AWS service. For example, an CloudFormation `CreateStack` call can result in additional API calls to Amazon EC2, Amazon RDS, Amazon EBS, or other services as required by the CloudFormation template. This behavior is normal and expected. You can identify if the action was taken by an AWS service with the `invokedby` field in the CloudTrail event.
